text: Every lesson in this chapter has bumped into the same two customers: total spend of nine thousand eight hundred and seven thousand four hundred, where the typical customer spends about one twenty-four. An outlier is far from the rest of the data. An anomaly is an outlier that also looks wrong for a reason. EDA's job is to find them, explain them, and decide what to do.

The IQR rule flags any value more than one point five times the interquartile range beyond the quartiles, the same rule a box plot uses for its whiskers. Here the upper fence is about four twenty-five point eight, and nineteen customers get flagged. Nineteen out of five hundred is too many to call them all errors; some are just big spenders.

A z-score measures standard deviations from the mean; a common cutoff is an absolute z of three. That flags only two rows here, with z-scores of about seventeen point four and thirteen. The z-score method is blunter, because the mean and standard deviation are themselves inflated by those same two extreme values.

See it in a box plot. All five hundred rows gives a squashed box with two dots far away. Remove just those two giants, and the plot reveals a normal-looking, right-skewed distribution with a scatter of ordinary high spenders.

A flag is a question, not a verdict. Spend per order is a good sanity check: the median is thirty-seven dollars, and seventy-five percent of customers are under forty-eight. The two suspicious rows hit twenty-four fifty and fourteen eighty per order, forty to sixty-six times typical. The other seventeen flagged rows top out around one thirty-four per order; they spend a lot because they order a lot, which is plausible.

Five options: keep it if it's real, fix it if you can find the true value, remove it if it's an error you can't fix, cap it at a quantile boundary to limit influence, or flag it and decide later. Whichever you choose, write it down.

The consequences are real. Mean spend is one eighty-eight with the two rows, one fifty-four without them. And the app-spends-more story from the bivariate lesson vanishes once they're excluded: app, store and web all land within six dollars of each other. Next: automated EDA tools that generate much of this exploration for you.
